newsitem.title: USA: Australia cuts official interest rates to 6.5 pct.
newsitem.headline: Australia cuts official interest rates to 6.5 pct.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) said on Wednesday it was cutting official interest rates by half a percentage point to 6.5 percent, citing an improved inflation outlook which provided scope for the economy to run faster.
The cut, which was widely expected, is the second this year after the central bank cut rates to 7.0 percent from 7.5 percent on July 31.
"It's a reward for low inflation and wage restraint," Prime Minister John Howard told reporters. Howard said the rate cut would help job creation and boost the Australian economy.
"It will encourage people to take more risks to invest, to have a go and all of that helps," Howard said.
The RBA said in a statement that it had decided at its monthly board meeting on Tuesday to cut interest rates.

"This decision was taken by the board yesterday in view of the improvement in the outlook for inflation, which has increased the scope for the economy to sustain a faster rate of growth," the bank said.
The bank said inflation had returned to its target range of two to three percent, adding that a firm exchange rate had helped ease inflationary pressures.
The bank said slower wages growth was the most significant factor in the favourable inflation outlook over the next year.
"The bank's view is that monetary policy should not stand in the way of higher growth if the economy has the capacity to achieve that growth without threatening the low inflation objective," it said.
Analysts estimate the Australian economy is growing at around three percent.
Economists had widely expected the rate cut, citing a need to stimulate the economy after recent weak economic data.

"It's a good move, a neccessary move and should ensure the economy will be OK in 1997," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia. "Any more than 0.5 point might have smacked of panic, so the size looks just right."
"It shows they're taking a softly, softly approach to monetary policy which should maintain its anti-inflation credibility with offshore investors," Koukoulas said.
But economists said there was still a chance of a further cut in rates either next month or early next year, as long as wages growth remained steady.
